questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.q: A body starts from rest and accelerates uniformly. The ratio of the distances covered in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd seconds is:
questions.solution:
Distance in the $n$th second: $s_{n} = u + \dfrac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$.

From rest, $s_{n} \propto (2n - 1)$, giving $1 : 3 : 5$.

The **total** distances after 1, 2, 3 s are in the ratio $1 : 4 : 9$ — the squares. Reading the question carefully is half the battle here.

questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.q: For a given speed of projection, the maximum range is obtained at an angle of:
questions.solution:
$R = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin 2\theta}{g}$, which is greatest when $\sin 2\theta = 1$, that is $\theta = \mathbf{45°}$.

Note also that $30°$ and $60°$ give the **same** range, since $\sin 60° = \sin 120°$ — a favourite examination point.

questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.q: A body of mass $2$ kg moving at $5$ m/s is brought to rest in $0.1$ s. The average force is:
questions.solution:
$F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{2 \times 5}{0.1} = \mathbf{100}$ N.

Doubling the stopping **time** would halve the force — the principle behind airbags and crumple zones.

questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.q: A body of mass $m$ moving with velocity $v$ has its speed doubled. Its kinetic energy becomes:
questions.solution:
$E_{k} = \tfrac12 mv^{2} \propto v^{2}$, so doubling $v$ gives **four** times the energy.

This is why a car's braking distance quadruples when its speed doubles.

questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.q: A body moving in a circle at constant speed has:
questions.solution:
The **direction** of the velocity changes continuously, so there is an acceleration — directed towards the centre.

$a = \dfrac{v^{2}}{r}$. The speed is constant; the velocity is not.

questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.q: The moment of inertia of a solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about a diameter is:
questions.solution:
$I = \mathbf{\dfrac25 MR^{2}}$ for a solid sphere about a diameter.

For comparison: a hollow sphere is $\tfrac23 MR^{2}$, a solid cylinder $\tfrac12 MR^{2}$, and a ring $MR^{2}$. The more mass sits far from the axis, the larger the moment of inertia — which is why a hoop rolls down a slope more slowly than a sphere.

questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.q: The escape velocity from the surface of a planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is:
questions.solution:
$v_{e} = \mathbf{\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}} = \sqrt{2gR}$, which is $11.2$ km/s for the Earth.

It is exactly $\sqrt2$ times the orbital velocity at the surface, and it is independent of the escaping body's mass.

questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.q: Young's modulus of a wire does not depend on its:
questions.solution:
Young's modulus is a property of the **material**, not of the specimen — so its length and cross-section do not affect it.

They do affect the **extension** for a given load, through $x = \dfrac{FL}{AE}$, but not $E$ itself.

questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.q: According to Bernoulli's theorem, where the velocity of a fluid is high, the pressure is:
questions.solution:
$p + \tfrac12\rho v^{2} + \rho gh$ is constant, so a **higher velocity means a lower pressure**.

It is why an aerofoil generates lift, why a spinning ball swings, and why two ships sailing close alongside are drawn together.

questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.q: The excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius $r$ and surface tension $T$ is:
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{\dfrac{4T}{r}}$ for a **soap bubble**, which has **two** surfaces — inner and outer.

A liquid **drop** has only one surface, so its excess pressure is $\dfrac{2T}{r}$. The factor of two is the whole point of the question.

questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.q: The time period of a simple pendulum of length $l$ on the Earth's surface is:
questions.solution:
$T = \mathbf{2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}}$, independent of the bob's **mass** and (for small swings) of the amplitude.

The independence of mass is what makes a pendulum a reliable clock, and its dependence on $g$ is how $g$ is measured.

questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.solution:
**Adiabatic** means $q = 0$ — no heat enters or leaves.

By the first law, $\Delta U = W$, so compressing a gas adiabatically **raises its temperature**. That is how a diesel engine ignites its fuel without a spark.
options: no heat is exchanged with the surroundings

questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.q: The average kinetic energy of a gas molecule depends only on:
questions.solution:
$\overline{E_{k}} = \tfrac32 kT$ — it depends on **absolute temperature alone**.

At the same temperature, hydrogen and oxygen molecules have the same average kinetic energy, so the lighter hydrogen moves much faster. That is what temperature **is**, microscopically.

questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.q: A stationary wave is formed by the superposition of two waves that have:
questions.solution:
Two waves of the **same frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions** — usually a wave and its own reflection.

The result has fixed **nodes** and **antinodes**, and transfers no energy, since no energy can cross a node.
options: the same frequency travelling in opposite directions

questions.chapter: Physics: Mechanics and Properties of Matter
questions.q: A source of sound approaches a stationary observer. The observed frequency is:
questions.solution:
**Higher** — the wavefronts are bunched up ahead of the approaching source, so the wavelength reaching the observer is shorter.

The pitch drops abruptly as the source passes, which is the familiar sound of an ambulance. The same effect on light gives the redshift of receding galaxies.
